INCIDENT REVIEW — INC-2091
Cascade Ledger, Payments Platform Engineering
Severity: SEV-2 | Status: Closed | Prepared by: Priya Ramanathan (Incident Commander)
Date of incident: March 14 | Report finalized: March 21

SUMMARY
On March 14, between 09:52 and 10:41 UTC, the payment processing pipeline experienced elevated error rates, with roughly 6% of transaction requests timing out during the 49-minute window. Customer-facing impact was moderate: most clients' retry logic succeeded within seconds, but approximately 2,300 transactions had to be manually reconciled by the settlements team over the following two days. This is the second production incident affecting the payments pipeline this quarter, after INC-1774 in February, which involved a database failover triggered by a stale DNS record ahead of a planned maintenance window. Engineering leadership specifically asked that this report distinguish the two clearly, since several support tickets filed after March 14 assumed the underlying cause was the same failover issue, which delayed initial customer communications by roughly twenty minutes while support leads double-checked with the on-call engineer.

TIMELINE
09:52 - Alerting fired for elevated p99 latency on the checkout API.
09:58 - On-call engineer Diego Salcedo acknowledged the page.
10:04 - Diego escalated to the ledger-writer service owners after ruling out upstream network issues.
10:15 - Tomasz Wieczorek joined the call and began reviewing the most recent deploy, a config-only push merged at 09:30 by a teammate covering for a colleague on leave.
10:23 - The config push was identified as the likely trigger and a rollback was initiated.
10:41 - Error rates returned to baseline; the incident was downgraded to monitoring status.
11:30 - Incident formally closed after thirty minutes of stable metrics.

ROOT CAUSE
The 09:30 config push reduced the ledger-writer service's downstream connection-pool timeout from 30 seconds to 5 seconds. The change was intended for an unrelated staging experiment and was accidentally bundled into the production config push by the covering teammate, who was unfamiliar with the repository layout. Under normal load this setting is harmless, but during the mid-morning traffic peak, calls from ledger-writer to its storage backend routinely take 6 to 9 seconds to complete, so the shortened timeout caused a cascade of retries and connection-pool exhaustion across the fleet. To be unambiguous for anyone comparing this to prior incidents: this was not caused by a database failover, and no failover occurred during this window. INC-1774's trigger, a DNS record that had not been refreshed before a planned failover, is unrelated to the connection-pool regression described here, even though both incidents happened to affect checkout latency and both were first noticed through the same p99 latency alert. Two contributing factors made the incident worse than it should have been. First, the config push went out without the peer review that team policy requires for any production change touching connection settings. Second, the paging threshold for checkout latency had been raised the prior week specifically to reduce alert noise from an unrelated flaky test, and that change delayed the page reaching Diego by roughly 22 minutes after error rates first crossed the old, more sensitive threshold.

For the record, since it came up twice during the retro: this incident was not a capacity shortfall, and it did not involve the ledger-reader service. Ledger-reader showed a brief, unrelated latency bump around 10:10 caused by a scheduled nightly batch job that had drifted into business hours; on-call ruled it out within minutes because its error budget was untouched.

CUSTOMER IMPACT AND METRICS
Total affected requests: 14,900. Requests that succeeded on retry without any manual action: 12,600. Transactions requiring manual settlement reconciliation: 2,300. No customer-reported financial loss was confirmed; three customers opened tickets asking whether card data had been exposed, and support confirmed no such exposure occurred, since this was purely a timeout cascade with no data access involved.

CONSIDERED BUT REJECTED
During the retro, the team discussed reverting the connection-pooling library entirely to the version used before last quarter's upgrade. This was rejected: the library itself was not at fault, only the timeout value shipped for the wrong environment, and a full revert would have re-introduced two connection leaks that the upgrade had already fixed.

ACTION ITEMS
1. Require review on all config-only pushes touching ledger-writer (owner: Tomasz, due March 28).
2. Revert the paging threshold change and add a separate, more sensitive alert for connection-pool exhaustion specifically (owner: Diego, due March 24).
3. Add a staging-versus-production config linter to catch this kind of cross-environment leakage before deploy (owner: Priya, due April 4).

SIGN-OFF
Approved by Priya Ramanathan and Hana Kobayashi, Director of Platform Engineering, on March 21.

MARROW BAY CREDIT UNION
Minutes of the Regular Meeting of the Board of Directors
Date: April 9 | Location: Main Branch Conference Room | Recorded by: Ines Duarte, Board Secretary

ATTENDANCE
Present: Grant Whitfield (Chair), Aisha Bello (Vice Chair), Noah Fitzgerald (Treasurer), Layla Haddad, Callum Boyd, Petra Novak. Absent with notice: Owen McAllister. Also present: Victor Okonkwo (CEO), Ines Duarte (Secretary, non-voting).

CALL TO ORDER
Chair Whitfield called the meeting to order at 6:02 p.m. and confirmed a quorum was present. The minutes of the March 12 meeting were approved without amendment.

OLD BUSINESS
Item 2: Elmhurst Branch Renovation, revisited. The Chair reminded the board that at the February meeting, a proposal to fully renovate the Elmhurst branch lobby and drive-through at a cost of $240,000 was brought to a vote and did not pass, with three directors citing concerns about committing that much of the facilities budget in a single year. Petra Novak asked whether the vendor quotes behind that figure were still valid; Victor Okonkwo confirmed the general contractor had agreed to hold pricing through June.

NEW BUSINESS
Item 4: Revised Elmhurst Branch Renovation Proposal. Victor Okonkwo presented a scaled-back proposal, developed with the same contractor, that deferred the drive-through canopy replacement to next fiscal year and focused this year's spending on the lobby, teller line, and ADA-compliant restroom. The revised proposal was presented to the board at $185,000. During discussion, Noah Fitzgerald moved to approve the $185,000 figure. Layla Haddad proposed an amendment to reduce the approved amount by $10,000 by using a less expensive flooring option that the contractor had also quoted, in order to leave additional headroom in the facilities reserve ahead of the planned Riverton exterior work later this year. The amendment passed 5-1, with Callum Boyd opposed. The amended motion, to approve $175,000 for the Elmhurst branch renovation using the reduced-cost flooring option, then passed unanimously, 6-0.

Item 5: Riverton Branch Exterior Signage. Victor Okonkwo requested approval of $40,000 for replacement of the Riverton branch's exterior signage and monument sign, both of which have been non-compliant with the county's updated visibility ordinance since a zoning change last year. Aisha Bello moved to approve; Grant Whitfield seconded. The motion passed unanimously, 6-0.

Item 6: Third-Party Auditor Engagement. Noah Fitzgerald presented a proposal to engage an outside firm, Dunmore & Ash LLP, to conduct the credit union's annual financial statement audit for the upcoming fiscal year, at a fixed fee of $22,500, replacing last year's auditor whose engagement letter expired. After brief discussion about Dunmore & Ash's credentials and references from two peer credit unions, Layla Haddad moved to approve the engagement; Petra Novak seconded. The motion passed 6-0.

Item 7: Downtown Branch Study. Callum Boyd raised the question of whether the underperforming Downtown branch should be considered for closure or relocation, citing declining foot traffic. After discussion, the board agreed this required more data than was available tonight. Grant Whitfield moved to table the matter and direct staff to prepare a traffic and deposit-trend report for the June meeting. The motion to table passed 6-0. No funds were approved and no closure decision was made.

PUBLIC COMMENT
Two members attended during the public comment period. One asked about extended hours at the Elmhurst branch once renovation is complete; the Chair noted that would be considered separately from the renovation budget itself.

TREASURER'S REPORT
Noah Fitzgerald reported the facilities reserve fund balance stood at $612,000 prior to tonight's approvals, and reminded the board that both the Elmhurst and Riverton approvals tonight would be drawn from that reserve, leaving an estimated $397,000 remaining for the fiscal year.

ADJOURNMENT
There being no further business, the meeting was adjourned at 7:41 p.m. Next regular meeting: May 14.

Minutes respectfully submitted by Ines Duarte, Board Secretary.

MASTER SERVICES AGREEMENT
Between Solmere Energy, Inc. ("Client") and Vantage Analytics LLC ("Vendor")
Effective Date: June 1

RECITALS
WHEREAS, Vendor provides subscription-based data-dashboard and reporting services; and
WHEREAS, Client wishes to engage Vendor to provide such services for Client's internal operations reporting; and
WHEREAS, the parties acknowledge that Vendor has previously contracted with other clients on similar terms, including a 2021 agreement with Thistledown Foods, Inc. under which the parties agreed to a flat liability cap of $50,000 regardless of fees paid, a structure the parties do NOT adopt here for the reasons set out in Section 6 below;
NOW, THEREFORE, the parties agree as follows.

1. DEFINITIONS
"Services" means the dashboard hosting, data-integration, and monthly reporting services described in Exhibit A. "Confidential Information" has the meaning given in Section 7. "Fees" means the amounts payable under Exhibit A.

2. SERVICES
Vendor shall provide the Services in accordance with the specifications in Exhibit A and shall use commercially reasonable efforts to maintain 99.5% uptime for the hosted dashboard, measured monthly.

3. FEES AND PAYMENT
Client shall pay Vendor the fees set out in Exhibit A within thirty (30) days of invoice. Late payments accrue interest at 1.5% per month.

4. TERM
This Agreement begins on the Effective Date and continues for an initial term of twelve (12) months, renewing automatically for successive twelve-month terms unless either party gives notice of non-renewal at least forty-five (45) days before the end of the then-current term.

5. TERMINATION
5.1 Termination for Convenience. Either party may terminate this Agreement for convenience upon sixty (60) days' prior written notice to the other party. An earlier draft of this Agreement circulated on May 3 permitted termination for convenience on thirty (30) days' notice; that draft language is superseded in its entirety by this Section 5.1.
5.2 Termination for Cause. Either party may terminate immediately if the other party materially breaches this Agreement and fails to cure such breach within fifteen (15) days of written notice describing the breach.

6. LIMITATION OF LIABILITY
Except for breaches of Section 7 (Confidentiality) or a party's indemnification obligations, each party's total aggregate liability arising out of or related to this Agreement shall not exceed the greater of (a) $75,000, or (b) the total Fees paid or payable by Client in the two (2) months immediately preceding the event giving rise to the claim. The parties considered and rejected mirroring the flat $50,000 cap used in Vendor's Thistledown Foods agreement, since Client's monthly fee under this Agreement is substantially higher than Thistledown Foods' and a flat cap of that size would have represented a smaller effective protection relative to fees paid. IN NO EVENT SHALL EITHER PARTY BE LIABLE FOR INDIRECT, INCIDENTAL, OR CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES.

7. CONFIDENTIALITY
Each party shall protect the other's Confidential Information using at least the same degree of care it uses for its own confidential information, and in no case less than reasonable care. This obligation survives termination for five (5) years.

8. GENERAL PROVISIONS
Notices under this Agreement must be in writing and delivered by email with read receipt or by certified mail. This Agreement is governed by the laws of the state in which Client is headquartered. This Agreement, together with Exhibit A, constitutes the entire agreement between the parties and supersedes all prior discussions, drafts, and proposals, including the May 3 draft referenced in Section 5.1.

SIGNATURES
For Solmere Energy, Inc.: Marisol Vega, VP Operations
For Vantage Analytics LLC: Elliot Ferris, Director of Client Contracts

EXHIBIT A — FEE SCHEDULE AND SERVICE SPECIFICATIONS
Monthly subscription fee: $12,500, covering hosting for up to 40 named dashboard users and up to 15 integrated data sources. Additional named users: $150/user/month. Additional data sources: $400/source/month. Optional quarterly business review: included at no additional charge. Support response target: 4 business hours for standard requests, 1 business hour for outages affecting the entire dashboard.

NORTHBRIDGE FREIGHT — INTERNAL AUDIT SUMMARY
Subject: Q1 Discretionary Departmental Spending Review
Prepared by: Internal Audit Office (Renata Silva, Lead Auditor)
Distribution: Finance Committee, Department Heads
Date Issued: April 18

PURPOSE AND SCOPE
This review examines discretionary spending by department for the first fiscal quarter (January-March) against the $10,000 per-quarter discretionary spending threshold established in Finance Policy FP-114. Discretionary spending, as defined by FP-114, excludes payroll, approved capital projects, and pre-negotiated vendor contracts; it covers items such as team events, non-contracted software subscriptions, and ad hoc consulting engagements. Any department that exceeds the $10,000 threshold in a quarter must submit a variance memo to the Finance Committee within ten business days of quarter close.

METHODOLOGY
The audit team reconciled every discretionary purchase order and expense reimbursement against departmental cost centers for the quarter, cross-checked against corporate card statements, and interviewed each department head about purchases over $1,000. Two purchase orders initially miscoded to the wrong cost center were reassigned during the review; the figures below reflect the corrected totals.

FINDINGS BY DEPARTMENT
Sales: $9,400 in discretionary spending, driven mainly by a client-appreciation event in February ($4,100) and a new CRM add-on subscription ($3,200). This is under the $10,000 threshold and required no variance memo.
Marketing: $10,050 in discretionary spending, primarily a trade-show sponsorship ($6,500) added late in the quarter after the original budget was set. This exceeds the threshold by $50. A variance memo was filed on April 2, within the required window.
Operations: $14,200 in discretionary spending, the largest overage this quarter, driven by emergency contractor support during the February ice storm ($9,800) that was not pre-negotiated and therefore does not qualify for the capital-project exclusion. This exceeds the threshold by $4,200. A variance memo was filed on April 3.
Legal: $3,000 in discretionary spending, entirely a one-time external counsel consultation. Well under threshold.
Facilities: $10,000 in discretionary spending exactly, for routine building maintenance items that came in precisely at budget. Because FP-114 requires a variance memo only when spending exceeds the threshold, and $10,000 does not exceed $10,000, Facilities was not required to file a memo, though the audit team flagged this as a department to watch next quarter given how close it ran to the limit.

DISCUSSION
Two departments, Marketing and Operations, exceeded the discretionary threshold this quarter and both filed timely variance memos as required. The Operations overage is attributable to a genuinely unplanned weather event and the audit team recommends no corrective action beyond the memo already filed. The Marketing overage is smaller in absolute terms but reflects a pattern: Marketing has been within $500 of the threshold in two of the last three quarters, and the audit team recommends the Finance Committee consider whether Marketing's discretionary budget structure needs revisiting.

PRIOR AUDIT FOLLOW-UP
Last year's Q1 audit made two recommendations. The first, to require itemized receipts for any single discretionary purchase over $250, was accepted and has been in effect since July. The second, to raise the departmental discretionary threshold from $10,000 to $15,000 per quarter to reduce the number of variance memos for routine overages, was reviewed by the Finance Committee in September and rejected; committee minutes note the concern that a higher threshold would reduce visibility into departmental spending patterns without a clear offsetting benefit.

RECOMMENDATIONS
1. Finance Committee to review Marketing's recurring near-threshold pattern.
2. Facilities to be included in next quarter's pre-close check-in given how close it ran to the limit.
3. No change recommended to the $10,000 threshold itself at this time, consistent with last year's decision.
4. Audit Office to repeat this same discretionary-spending review next quarter using the identical methodology, so trends across departments remain comparable year over year.

DISTRIBUTION AND NEXT STEPS
This summary was distributed to the Finance Committee and all five department heads named above on the issue date. Any department head who disputes a figure in this summary has five business days to raise the discrepancy with the Audit Office before the report is filed as final with the Finance Committee's records.

Signed, Renata Silva, Lead Auditor, Internal Audit Office.

ANCHORLINE SHIPPING — WAREHOUSE SAFETY INCIDENT REPORT
Facility: Port Calder Distribution Center | Report No. WH-SIR-0447
Incident Date: September 5 | Report Date: September 19
Prepared by: Safety Committee (Chair: Wanjiru Kamau)

INCIDENT SUMMARY
At approximately 2:15 p.m. on September 5, forklift operator Marcus Oduya, while transporting a pallet through the Zone C blind corner, narrowly avoided colliding with pedestrian employee Theo Marsh, who was walking from the break room back to the picking floor. Theo was not struck; the forklift's load shifted and one carton fell, causing no injury. This is classified as a near-miss under WH-9 reporting requirements and was investigated accordingly.

WITNESS STATEMENTS
Theo Marsh stated he did not hear the forklift's horn before stepping around the corner. Marcus Oduya stated he sounded the horn but was traveling faster than the posted 5 mph zone limit, which he attributed to trying to finish the pallet run before his shift ended. A second operator working nearby, Selin Aydin, did not witness the near-miss directly but noted the Zone C corner has limited sightlines and has "always felt tight."

EQUIPMENT AND ENVIRONMENT REVIEW
The forklift involved (Unit F-12) was inspected by an outside technician on September 6 and found to be in full working order, with brakes, horn, and steering all within spec; mechanical failure was ruled out as a factor. Lighting levels in Zone C were measured and found to meet the facility's code requirement of 30 foot-candles at floor level; inadequate lighting was also ruled out.

CERTIFICATION REVIEW
Per policy WH-9, all forklift operators must hold a current certification, valid for 24 months from the date of renewal, and may not operate equipment with an expired certification under any circumstance. Marcus Oduya's certification was last renewed on July 2, 2023, meaning it expired on July 2, 2025, roughly two months before this incident. Marcus was therefore operating Unit F-12 without a valid certification at the time of the near-miss. For comparison, Selin Aydin's certification was renewed January 15, 2024 and remains valid through January 15, 2026; her certification status is not at issue in this incident and is noted here only because her statement is quoted above.

SCHEDULING REVIEW
The committee also reviewed Marcus's schedule for the week of the incident and found he had worked four consecutive 12-hour shifts immediately before September 5, two more consecutive long shifts than WH-9's fatigue-management guideline recommends without a rest day. The committee considers this a contributing factor to the speed violation described in his statement, though not the root cause.

ROOT CAUSE DETERMINATION
The committee determines the root cause of this near-miss to be Marcus Oduya operating forklift equipment with an expired certification, compounded by traveling above the posted speed limit in a low-visibility zone. Mechanical failure and inadequate lighting are explicitly ruled out as causes.

DISCUSSION OF PROPOSED RESPONSES
Committee member Rafael Obi proposed mandatory drug and alcohol testing for all operators involved in any near-miss incident, regardless of apparent cause. After discussion, the full safety board rejected this proposal 5-1, noting nothing in the equipment review, witness statements, or certification review suggested impairment, and that blanket testing without cause was inconsistent with the facility's existing testing policy. Separately, the committee discussed whether to move from 24-month to annual recertification for all operators facility-wide. This was not adopted; the board agreed only to have HR study the cost and scheduling impact further, with a recommendation due at the November safety meeting.

RECOMMENDATIONS ADOPTED
1. Marcus Oduya to complete recertification before returning to forklift duty, and to be retrained specifically on Zone C horn-and-yield procedure.
2. Facilities to install additional convex mirrors at the Zone C blind corner by October 1.
3. Warehouse scheduling to adopt a cap of two consecutive 12-hour shifts before a mandatory rest day, effective immediately.

Approved by the Safety Committee, September 19. Distribution: Facility Manager, HR, Operations Director.

Grants Committee Meeting Minutes
Date: October 3 | Recorded by: Miriam Castellano

Dahlia Prentiss presented five applications received before the September 15 deadline, in the order they were received.

1. Riverside Youth Arts — requested $20,000 for a mural and after-school printmaking program. The committee discussed the strength of the organization's prior-year reporting and agreed the request was well-justified but slightly high relative to the group's demonstrated capacity to spend within one cycle. Simon Achebe moved to approve $18,000, a reduction of $2,000 from the request, with the difference noted as available for a supplemental request next cycle if needed. The motion passed 5-0.

2. Coastal Robotics Club — requested $25,000 for competition equipment and travel. Rosalind Kanu noted the application was missing an itemized travel budget, which the committee needs to evaluate cost-effectiveness. Nora Lindqvist moved to table the application and request the missing itemization, rather than deny it outright, so it can be reconsidered without waiting for the next full cycle. The motion to table passed 4-1, Alistair Byrne opposed on the grounds that tabling creates uncertainty for the applicant. No funds were approved for this application at this meeting.

3. Elder Neighbors Network — requested $12,000 for a volunteer-driver transportation program. Given the funds already committed to Riverside Youth Arts, Felix Marchetti proposed approving a reduced amount of $9,000 to keep the cycle within budget while still supporting the program's core routes. Alistair Byrne moved to approve $9,000; Rosalind Kanu seconded. The motion passed 5-0.

4. Greenway Trail Alliance — requested $5,000 for trail signage. Dahlia Prentiss noted during due diligence that the organization's 501(c)(3) application is still pending with the state and has not yet been granted, which fails the committee's baseline eligibility requirement for fiscal sponsorship or registered nonprofit status. 5. Lakeside Literacy Project — requested $7,500 for adult literacy tutoring materials and tutor stipends. This confidentiality obligation survives termination of employment for five (5) years, regardless of the reason for termination.

2. NON-COMPETITION
For a period of twelve (12) months following the termination of Employee's employment with Cobalt Peak, for any reason, Employee agrees not to accept employment with, consult for, or hold an ownership interest greater than 2% in any company that the parties agree constitutes a "Direct Competitor," defined narrowly as a company whose primary product is enterprise data-visualization software marketed to companies with more than 500 employees. 3. NON-SOLICITATION

This Addendum is governed by the laws of the state listed in Employee's personnel file. This severability approach is why outside counsel preferred rewriting Section 2 outright rather than leaving the original 24-month figure in place for a court to modify later.

8. SURVIVAL
Sections 1 (Confidentiality), 2 (Non-Competition), 3 (Non-Solicitation), and 6 (Remedies) survive termination of employment according to their own stated durations; Section 1's five-year survival period is the longest of the obligations in this Addendum and is calculated from the termination date, not the Effective Date above.

ALDERPOINT HEALTH — INFORMATION SECURITY AUDIT REPORT
Annual External Penetration Test and Vulnerability Assessment
Conducted by: Stonebridge Security Partners | Report Date: November 8
Engagement Lead: Consuela Marques

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Stonebridge Security Partners conducted the annual external penetration test and internal vulnerability scan for Alderpoint Health's IT environment between October 14 and October 25. This year's assessment covered five in-scope systems: the patient portal, the billing system, the internal wiki, the backup server, and the scheduling system. Each finding is rated Critical, High, Medium, or Low following Alderpoint's standard severity rubric, which weighs both exploitability and potential impact on protected health information.

METHODOLOGY
The assessment combined automated scanning with manual verification of any finding rated Medium or above, to reduce false positives. Testers were given no internal credentials for the external-facing systems (black-box testing) and limited internal credentials for internal-only systems (grey-box testing), consistent with prior years' methodology to keep results comparable year over year. Findings below are ordered by system rather than by severity, since Alderpoint's internal tracking dashboard groups remediation tickets by system owner.

FINDINGS
Patient Portal (external-facing, black-box tested): Rated CRITICAL. Testers found the portal's login endpoint still accepted TLS 1.0 connections despite a company-wide mandate to disable protocols older than TLS 1.2, and found no rate limiting on login attempts, allowing an automated credential-stuffing attack to be simulated successfully against a test account within 40 minutes. Because this system handles patient authentication and can expose protected health information, this combination of findings receives the highest severity rating this year.

Billing System (internal-only, grey-box tested): Rated MEDIUM. Testers found that certain billing reports could be exported by any authenticated internal user regardless of department, rather than being restricted to the finance team, which is a data-minimization concern but requires internal network access and valid credentials to exploit, limiting its severity relative to the patient portal finding.

Internal Wiki (internal-only, grey-box tested): Rated LOW. An outdated plugin was identified with a known but low-severity cross-site scripting issue affecting only the wiki's comment feature, which is rarely used and contains no patient data.

Backup Server (internal-only, grey-box tested): Rated MEDIUM. Backup archive files were found to be encrypted at rest correctly, but the encryption key rotation schedule had lapsed eight months past its required annual rotation, which is a control gap even though no evidence of key compromise was found.

Scheduling System: Not assessed as part of this year's in-scope findings. For continuity, this report notes that last year's audit found a High-severity authentication bypass in the scheduling system; that finding was remediated by the vendor's patch in February and verified fixed by Stonebridge in a limited-scope retest in March. It is not a current-year finding and should not be counted among this year's open items.

RISK RANKING THIS YEAR
1. Patient Portal — Critical
2. Billing System — Medium
3. Backup Server — Medium
4. Internal Wiki — Low
(Scheduling System: prior-year finding, remediated, not re-assessed this cycle)

REMEDIATION TIMELINE REQUESTED
Alderpoint's CISO, Gideon Farley, has committed to the following remediation windows: Patient Portal TLS and rate-limiting fixes within 15 business days given the Critical rating; Billing System export restriction within 45 days; Backup Server key rotation within 30 days; Internal Wiki plugin update within 90 days given its Low rating and limited exposure.

AUDITOR'S NOTE
Consuela Marques added a note recommending that next year's scope be expanded to include the scheduling system again, given how quickly authentication issues can resurface in that system's history, even though this year's engagement contract did not include it in scope.

SIGN-OFF
Report reviewed and accepted by Gideon Farley, Chief Information Security Officer, Alderpoint Health, November 8.

REDWING INSURANCE — PRIVACY INCIDENT REVIEW
Incident Reference: PRIV-0316 | Classification: Confirmed data exposure, low severity per regulatory matrix
Prepared by: Privacy Office (Lead: Tariq Idris) | Report Date: May 30

BACKGROUND
On May 11, a customer service representative discovered that a misconfigured export job in the policy-quote subsystem had, since April 22, been generating quote-comparison PDF reports that briefly included the full name, partial address, and quoted premium of a different customer than the one requesting the quote, due to a caching bug that served a previous session's data under certain timing conditions. The Privacy Office was notified the same day and began an investigation under the company's incident response plan.

INITIAL ESTIMATE
On May 12, based on a quick review of export volumes during the affected window, the Privacy Office reported to executive leadership a preliminary estimate that "approximately 3,000" customer records may have been affected, and leadership was briefed on that basis pending a full log analysis. This preliminary figure was explicitly flagged at the time as a rough upper bound, not a confirmed count, pending detailed review.

DETAILED INVESTIGATION
Between May 12 and May 24, the Privacy Office worked with the engineering team to reconstruct affected sessions from application logs rather than relying on export volume alone. This analysis found that the caching bug only manifested under a narrow timing condition, roughly a 400-millisecond overlap window between two customers' quote requests hitting the same cache node, which was far less common than the initial volume-based estimate assumed. The confirmed, log-verified count of customer records where another customer's data was actually exposed in a generated PDF is 1,240. The Privacy Office considers this the authoritative figure for this incident, superseding the May 12 preliminary estimate.

SCOPE CLARIFICATION
This incident affected only the policy-quote subsystem, which generates comparison PDFs during the quoting flow. It did not affect the claims-processing subsystem. For unrelated context: the claims-processing subsystem did experience a separate, minor display bug during the same week, where adjuster notes occasionally failed to save on the first attempt; that issue was logged separately as INC-2240 and required no privacy notification, since no customer data was exposed, exchanged, or lost. The two issues are unrelated and should not be conflated, though both were reported internally in the same week and initial triage briefly treated them as possibly connected before ruling that out on May 13.

INDUSTRY CONTEXT
For background only, the Privacy Office noted that Marrow Bay Credit Union experienced a significant, unrelated data breach in 2019 that was widely covered in trade press and prompted several insurers, including Redwing, to review their own caching and session-isolation practices at the time. That 2019 event did not cause or contribute to this incident; it is referenced here only because two directors asked whether this incident was "the same kind of thing" they remembered reading about.

REGULATORY NOTIFICATION
Because the confirmed count and nature of the exposure met the threshold in the applicable state's breach notification law, Redwing notified the state insurance regulator within 72 hours of the confirmed count being finalized on May 24, consistent with the statutory requirement. Affected customers were notified by mail beginning May 29.

REMEDIATION
The caching bug was patched on May 13, before the detailed investigation concluded, eliminating any ongoing exposure risk while the investigation into historical scope continued. Engineering added a session-isolation integration test to the deployment pipeline to catch this class of bug before future releases.

CONCLUSION
The confirmed scope of this incident is 1,240 affected customer records in the policy-quote subsystem, down from the preliminary 3,000-record estimate reported on May 12. Regulatory notification was completed within the required window based on the confirmed count.

Approved by Tariq Idris, Privacy Office Lead, and countersigned by General Counsel, May 30.

MEMBER COMMENTS
Several members asked about the timeline for the roof inspection bids; Amara Chukwu committed to having at least three bids by the November board meeting, with a special membership meeting to follow afterward if a vote on the special assessment is needed before next year's annual meeting.

ADJOURNMENT
There being no further business, President Byrne adjourned the meeting at 8:47 p.m.

Minutes respectfully submitted by Keiko Sano, HOA Secretary, and approved as recorded by the Board on September 20.
